questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to use an incentive spirometer after abdominal surgery. Which client action shows correct understanding?

opts.t: Exhale forcefully into the mouthpiece 10 times each hour.
opts.r: The client inhales through an incentive spirometer; forceful exhalation does not expand the lungs.

opts.t: Sit upright, seal the lips around the mouthpiece, and inhale slowly until the marker rises.
opts.r: Correct. Upright positioning and a slow, sustained inhalation promote alveolar expansion and help prevent postoperative atelectasis.

opts.t: Use the spirometer only when shortness of breath occurs.
opts.r: The device is used regularly while awake as prescribed, not only after symptoms develop.

opts.t: Breathe rapidly through the mouthpiece to raise the marker quickly.
opts.r: Rapid inhalation is less effective; a slow, deep breath is needed to promote sustained lung expansion.

questions.tip: Incentive spirometer = sit up, inhale slowly and deeply, hold briefly, then repeat regularly while awake.
questions.pearl: Slow and steady raises the spirometer and opens alveoli.

questions.stem: Which action by the nurse is most effective for preventing a catheter-associated urinary tract infection in a client with an indwelling urinary catheter?

opts.t: Disconnect the drainage tubing daily to clean the connection.
opts.r: Disconnecting tubing breaks the closed system and increases infection risk.

opts.t: Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and maintain a closed drainage system.
opts.r: Correct. Dependent drainage and an intact closed system reduce backflow and contamination.

opts.t: Irrigate the catheter every shift with sterile saline.
opts.r: Routine irrigation is not indicated and can introduce organisms; it is done only for a specific order or indication.

opts.t: Apply antibiotic ointment to the urinary meatus with every shift assessment.
opts.r: Routine antibiotic ointment is not a CAUTI-prevention measure and can contribute to irritation or resistance.

questions.tip: CAUTI prevention: use a catheter only when necessary, keep a closed system, keep the bag below the bladder, and remove it as soon as possible.

questions.stem: A nurse empties a Jackson-Pratt drain after abdominal surgery. Which action is correct after measuring the drainage?

opts.t: Compress the bulb before replacing the plug to reestablish suction.
opts.r: Correct. Compressing the bulb before closing it creates the gentle suction needed for the drain to function.

opts.t: Leave the bulb expanded so the drainage can flow by gravity.
opts.r: An expanded bulb does not provide the prescribed closed-suction drainage.

opts.t: Clamp the tubing tightly between emptying episodes.
opts.r: Routine clamping can obstruct drainage and is not performed unless specifically prescribed.

opts.t: Place the drain on the bed above the insertion site.
opts.r: The drain is kept below the insertion site to promote drainage and prevent backflow.

questions.tip: JP drain: empty, measure, compress, recap, and keep below the insertion site.

questions.stem: A client receives medications through a feeding tube and has continuous enteral feeding prescribed. Which action should the nurse take when administering the medications?

opts.t: Crush all medications together and mix them into the feeding formula.
opts.r: Mixing medications with formula risks tube occlusion, drug interactions, and inaccurate dosing; medications are given separately.

opts.t: Verify that each medication is safe to crush, administer medications separately, and flush the tube between medications.
opts.r: Correct. The nurse verifies formulation safety, administers one medication at a time, and flushes as prescribed to maintain patency and prevent interactions.

opts.t: Add the medications directly to the drainage bag so they infuse slowly.
opts.r: A drainage bag is not used to administer medications and this would be unsafe.

opts.t: Skip all water flushes to avoid fluid overload.
opts.r: Flushes are essential for patency and medication delivery; fluid restriction requires an individualized plan, not omission of prescribed flushes.

questions.tip: Never crush enteric-coated or extended-release medications. Give tube medications one at a time with ordered flushes.

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse take when communicating with a client who has a hearing aid and moderate hearing loss?

opts.t: Stand behind the client and speak loudly into the affected ear.
opts.r: Speaking from behind prevents the client from using facial cues or lip reading and may startle the client.

opts.t: Face the client, reduce background noise, and speak clearly at a normal pace.
opts.r: Correct. Direct visual contact, reduced noise, and clear normal-paced speech support communication without distorting words.

opts.t: Use complex medical terms so the client can focus on key words.
opts.r: Simple, direct language supports understanding; jargon adds confusion.

opts.t: Remove the hearing aid before teaching to prevent distraction.
opts.r: The nurse should verify that the hearing aid is present, working, and in place unless removal is needed for care.

questions.tip: For hearing loss: face the client, speak clearly, lower background noise, and confirm understanding.

questions.stem: An older adult taking an antihypertensive reports dizziness when rising from bed. Which instruction should the nurse give first?

opts.t: Stand quickly to help the blood pressure adjust faster.
opts.r: Rapid position changes can worsen orthostatic hypotension and increase fall risk.

opts.t: Sit at the bedside with the feet dangling before standing.
opts.r: Correct. Changing positions gradually allows assessment for dizziness and reduces the risk of a fall from orthostatic hypotension.

opts.t: Avoid all fluids until the dizziness resolves.
opts.r: Dehydration can worsen orthostatic symptoms; fluid guidance depends on the client's condition and prescription.

opts.t: Walk without assistance to build tolerance.
opts.r: The client should request assistance until safety and stability with ambulation are established.

questions.tip: Orthostatic safety: lie to sit, pause, dangle, stand with help, then reassess for dizziness.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after packed red blood cells are started, a client reports chills and low back pain. Which action should the nurse take first?

opts.t: Slow the transfusion and reassess the client in 15 minutes.
opts.r: Continuing a suspected transfusion reaction, even at a slower rate, can worsen a life-threatening event.

opts.t: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with normal saline using new tubing.
opts.r: Correct. The nurse stops the blood immediately, maintains venous access with normal saline using new tubing, assesses the client, and then follows the reaction protocol.

opts.t: Administer acetaminophen and continue the transfusion.
opts.r: Medication may be prescribed after evaluation, but the transfusion must be stopped first.

opts.t: Discard the blood bag and tubing before notifying the provider.
opts.r: The blood bag and tubing are retained and sent according to policy for investigation; they are not discarded.

questions.tip: Suspected transfusion reaction: stop blood, keep vein open with normal saline using new tubing, assess, notify, and follow policy.

questions.stem: While receiving a cleansing enema, a client reports severe cramping and asks the nurse to stop. Which action should the nurse take?

opts.t: Increase the flow rate so the procedure ends faster.
opts.r: Increasing the flow can intensify cramping and cause injury.

opts.t: Temporarily clamp the tubing and encourage slow deep breathing.
opts.r: Correct. Temporarily stopping the flow can reduce cramping; the nurse then reassesses and resumes more slowly if tolerated.

opts.t: Remove the tubing immediately and document that the client refused treatment.
opts.r: Severe or persistent symptoms require stopping and assessment, but brief cramping can often be managed by temporarily reducing the flow.

opts.t: Place the client supine and elevate the legs.
opts.r: The left lateral position supports enema flow; supine positioning with elevated legs does not relieve the issue.

questions.tip: For enema cramping, slow or briefly stop the flow; do not force the solution.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a new colostomy 24 hours after surgery. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?

opts.t: A stoma that is moist and beefy red.
opts.r: A moist, red to pink stoma is an expected finding that indicates perfusion.

opts.t: Mild edema of the stoma.
opts.r: Some swelling is common during the early postoperative period.

opts.t: A stoma that is dusky purple and dry.
opts.r: Correct. A dusky, purple, or black stoma may indicate impaired perfusion or ischemia and requires immediate assessment and notification.

opts.t: Small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the pouching system.
opts.r: A small amount of early postoperative drainage can be expected; the nurse monitors the amount and character.

questions.tip: A healthy stoma is moist and red/pink. Dusky, pale, blue, purple, or black means impaired perfusion.

questions.stem: A client has just returned from a thyroidectomy and is awake. Which position is most appropriate for the nurse to use?

opts.t: Supine with the neck extended on a small pillow.
opts.r: Neck extension can increase tension at the operative site and is avoided.

opts.t: Semi-Fowler position with the head and neck supported in neutral alignment.
opts.r: Correct. Semi-Fowler positioning reduces neck edema and supports breathing while neutral alignment avoids strain on the incision.

opts.t: Trendelenburg position with the head below the heart.
opts.r: Trendelenburg can worsen upper-airway edema and is not appropriate after thyroid surgery.

opts.t: Prone position with the head turned to one side.
opts.r: Prone positioning places pressure and strain near the surgical area and is not indicated.

questions.tip: After thyroidectomy, elevate the head of bed and support the head and neck in neutral alignment.
